ཞེས་སྨྲས་པས། འདིར་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་འགག་པ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་དགག་གོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེ་ལ་དོན་དམ་པར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བ་རྫས་དང་དངོས་པོ་དང་གཞིའི་སྒོ་ནས་དགག་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱི་བདེན་པ་ལ་གནས་ནས་དོན་དམ་པའི་ཡུལ་ལ་དགག་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། 
དོན་དམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དགག་པའི་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱང་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ལ་ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པར་བྱ་བ་ཕྱོགས་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཅན་ཡིན་ནོ། །བདག་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་ངེས་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཏེ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཡོད་པའི་
ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཏེ་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཡིན་ནོ། །དཔེར་ན་ཤེས་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་བཞིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་དཔེ་སྟེ། ཆོས་མཐུན་པའི་དཔེ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལ་ནང་གི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བདག་གིས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་ཤིང་གནས་སུ་བྱས་པའོ། །བདག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚམས་ལ་བདག་
གིར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ། ཡོ་བྱད་གྱ་ནོམ་པ་དང་། རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་དག་དང་པོར་བྱས་ནས། ཡོ་བྱད་ངན་པ་དང་ཁྱོན་ཆུང་ངུའི་བར་དག་ལ་བདག་གིར་བྱེད་པས་བདག་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །བདག་དེས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་ཤིང་གནས་སུ་བྱས་པ་ནི་ནང་གི་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སེམས་དང་སེམས་
ལས་འབྱུང་བ་རྣམས་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འབྱུང་བ་དང་། མཆེད་ཅིང་རྒྱས་པར་བྱེད་པས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་ཏེ་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། མིག་དང་རྣ་བ་དང་སྣ་དང་ལྕེ་དང་ལུས་དང་ཡིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་རྣམས་སོ། །ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནི་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པར་བྱ་བ་ཕྱོགས་ཏེ་ཆོས་ཅན་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པར་
བྱ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གང་ལ་མི་དམིགས་པ་ལས་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པར་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་དང་། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ལས་མི་རྟག་པར་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་ལས་རྒྱུ་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པའི་གཞི་སྟེ། སྐབས་འདིར་ནི་གང་ལ་བདག་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པར་བྱ་བའི་གཞི་ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་
སོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཕྱོགས་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ཕྱོགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་ཅན་བསྡུས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ཏེ། སྐབས་འདིར་ནི་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་བདག་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་། གང་ལ་དེ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་གཞིའི་ཆོས་ཅན་ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་གཉིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཕྱོགས་

Having stated this, the point here is that cessation without birth is also negated in the ultimate sense. Regarding the phrase "in the ultimate sense," this means the negation of birth from the perspective of substance, entity, and substrate in the ultimate sense. Furthermore, by relying on the relative truth <term>samvrti-satya</term> <gloss>conventional reality</gloss>, one negates things within the domain of the ultimate. However, within the ultimate itself, there is no expression, and thus the convention of negation does not exist.

The phrase "the internal sense sources" <term>ayatana</term> <gloss>bases of perception</gloss> refers to the subject of the inference <note>original: "dharmin"</note>. The phrase "certainly do not arise from themselves" refers to the predicate to be proven <note>original: "sadhya-dharma"</note> in the inference. The phrase "because they exist" refers to the reason <term>hetu</term> <gloss>logical ground</gloss> for the proof, which is the property of the subject. The phrase "just as, for example, the existence of cognition" is the example <note>original: "drstanta"</note>, specifically an example of similar class.

In this context, "internal" refers to that which is blessed and made into a residence by the "self." The "self" refers to that which takes ownership within a boundary. Beginning with excellent and extensive possessions down to poor and small items, that which takes ownership of them is called the "self." That which is blessed and made into a residence by that self is called "internal."

The "sense sources" <term>ayatana</term> are so called because they cause the mind and mental factors to arise, emerge, spread, and expand. These are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. "The internal sense sources" is the subject of the inference.

Regarding "the subject of inference," it is the basis for inferring non-existence from non-perception, inferring impermanence from the essential nature, or inferring a cause from its effect. In this specific context, the basis of the inference—that which does not arise from itself—is the internal sense sources.

This is called the "thesis" <term>paksha</term>. The term "thesis" refers to the combination of the predicate and the subject. In this context, the thesis is the combination of the predicate to be proven, which is "not arising from self," and the subject that serves as the basis for that proof, which is "the internal sense sources."

<summary>This page provides a linguistic and logical breakdown of a syllogism concerning the ultimate non-birth of internal sense sources. It defines technical terms of Buddhist logic such as the subject, predicate, and reason while clarifying the relationship between the self and the internal bases of perception.</summary>
<keywords>ultimate truth, internal sense sources, ayatana, logic, inference, dharmin, sadhya, self, birth, negation</keywords>

བླངས་པ་ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དབུ་མ་པས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཁས་བླངས་པ་ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་དག་ཡིན་པ་རྣམས་ཏེ། དེ་རྣམས་འདིར་ཆོས་ཅན་དུ་བྱའོ། །རྒྱུ་མེད་པ་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་དེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཁས་བླངས་པ་
ནང་གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་དེ་རྣམས་རྒྱུ་མེད་པ་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་འདིར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་ཡིན་ནོ། །སྤྱི་དང་ཁྱད་པར་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སྤྱི་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་དྲུག་པོ་དག་ལ་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་
ཅེས་བྱ་བ་སྤྱི་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་དྲུག་པོ་དག་ལ། མིག་དང་། རྣ་བ་དང་། སྣ་དང་། ལྕེ་དང་། ལུས་དང་། ཡིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་སོ་སོའི་ཁྱད་པར་ཉིད་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡང་ན་སྤྱི་ཉིད་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་

<meta>This page contains a commentary on Madhyamaka logic, specifically focusing on the syllogism used to prove that phenomena do not arise without causes.</meta>

The statement "there is no arising from no cause" is the <term>sadhya</term> <gloss>the property to be proven</gloss>. The statement "because of possessing both generality and particularity" is the <term>hetu</term> <gloss>the reason or logical mark</gloss>. The statement "for example, like a sprout" should be applied as the <term>udaharana</term> <gloss>the example</gloss>.

Regarding that, "internal <term>ayatanas</term> <gloss>sense sources</gloss> accepted as <term>samvrti</term> <gloss>conventional reality</gloss>" refers to those things accepted as conventional by the <term>Madhyamaka</term> <gloss>Followers of the Middle Way</gloss> such as the eye and the other sense sources; these are the subjects of the argument here. 

"There is no arising from no cause" means that those internal sense sources accepted conventionally do not arise without a cause; this is the property to be proven here.

Regarding the phrase "because of possessing both generality and particularity," the part "possessing generality" means that among the six sense sources—the eye and so forth—there exists the generality called "sense source." 

"Possessing particularity" means that among those six sense sources—the eye and so forth—there exist the individual particularities called "eye," "ear," "nose," "tongue," "body," and "mind."

Alternatively, "possessing generality" means that for all sense sources, there is the generality of being called "sense sources" and again "sense sources." "Possessing particularity" means that there are particularities such as "human sense sources," "divine sense sources," and "animal sense sources."

The term "itself" <note>Tibetan: nyid</note> refers to the fact that things which are general and particular are themselves the generality and particularity. "Because of possessing" means possessing that very generality and particularity; this is the logical reason here.

The phrase "for example, like a sprout" is used because a sprout also possesses a general nature in that all sprouts are called "sprout," and it also possesses particularity such as "rice sprout" and "barley sprout." For example, because a sprout conventionally possesses both generality and particularity, it does not arise without a cause. This is because it arises from a chain of beginningless causes, and thus it is not without a cause.

<summary>This text explains a logical syllogism used in Madhyamaka philosophy to demonstrate that internal sense sources arise from causes rather than causelessly. It breaks down the argument into its formal components: the property to be proven, the reason based on generality and particularity, and the supporting example of a sprout.</summary>
<keywords>Madhyamaka, logic, syllogism, sense sources, ayatana, causality, generality and particularity, sprout example</keywords>

བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པར་འདོད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁྱེད་ཅག་གོ། །སྡེ་པ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་དང་། བྱེ་བྲག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་མིང་ཐ་དད་པས་ཐ་དད་པ་གང་དག་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་དེ་དག་ཉིད་དུ་འདུས་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར། རྐྱེན་ལྔ་པ་ནི་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་ངེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་བརྗོད་
དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བས་ནི་འདི་སྐད་བསྟན་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་པ་ཁ་ཅིག་གིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་མདུན་དུ་སྐྱེས་པ་དང་། ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་དག་ཡིན་པ་དང་བྱེ་བྲག་པ་དག་གིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་གཉིས་དང་གསུམ་དང་བཞི་སྦྱོར་བར་བྱེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། ཡུལ་དང་དབང་པོ་དང་
བློ་དང་རྩོལ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་གང་དག་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་མིང་ཐ་དད་པར་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཐ་དད་པར་ཟད་ཀྱི། མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་ནི་དེ་དག་ལ་ཐ་དད་པ་མེད་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རྐྱེན་བཞི་པོ་དེ་དག་ཉིད་དུ་འདུས་སོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ལྟ་ཡིན་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། རྐྱེན་ལྔ་པ་ནི་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་
ངེས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་བརྗོད་དོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་དག་གཞན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པ་ཁོ་ནར་མི་རིགས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡང་ན་གཞན་དུ་རྣམ་པར་བརྟག་སྟེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྐབས་ཉིད་སྟོན་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རང་གི་སྡེ་པ་དག་གིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྟགས་པ་རྒྱུ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རྐྱེན་བཞི་པོ་དེ་དག་དཔྱད་ན། དོན་དམ་པར་གཞན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པ་ཁོ་ནར་མི་རིགས་

For those who teach that things arise from other factors, it is necessary to examine this further. This refers to the proponents of our own Buddhist schools, specifically the <term>Vaibhashika</term> <gloss>Great Exposition school</gloss> and the <term>Sautrantika</term> <gloss>Sutra school</gloss>. For the sake of those who teach that things arise from factors other than themselves, this verse should be examined in another way. One must investigate whether it is logical or illogical for things to arise from other factors in conjunction with those very conditions. The point is that this must be analyzed through reasoning.

In this context, it is said:

There are four conditions: the cause,
The object, the immediate,
And likewise the dominant condition.

You <note>referring to the proponents of the Buddhist schools mentioned above</note> assert that these are what produce functional things. Some other Buddhist schools have their own conceptualizations, and non-Buddhist schools like the <term>Vaisheshika</term> <gloss>Particularist school</gloss> have their own conceptualizations under different names. However, because those are all included within these same definitions, it is stated as a certainty:

A fifth condition does not exist.

This demonstrates the following: some Buddhists conceptualize conditions such as "pre-arisen," "existent," or "non-existent." The <term>Vaisheshika</term> conceptualize the conjunction of two, three, or four atoms. They also conceptualize objects, sense faculties, cognition, and effort. While these are presented as distinct through different names, they are not distinct in terms of their actual definitions. Therefore, they are all included within those four conditions. Because this is the case, it is stated as a certainty that "a fifth condition does not exist."

In ultimate truth, it is illogical for these conditions to be strictly "other" than the result. This indicates the context for further investigation. If one analyzes the four conditions like "cause" as conceptualized by our own schools, it is illogical and untenable for them to be strictly "other" in an ultimate sense.

If the opponent asks, "How so?" the following is stated:

The essence of functional things
Does not exist in conditions and such.

"Of functional things" refers to internal things, as well as those that are subtle or gross. Regarding internal <note>the text breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

<summary>This page analyzes the four conditions of causation from the perspective of Madhyamaka philosophy, arguing that all proposed causal factors fit into four categories and lack inherent existence. It challenges the Buddhist Vaibhashika and Sautrantika views that things arise from factors truly external or "other" to themselves.</summary>

གཞན་པ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དེ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དཔེ་ནི་དེའི་དབང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཆོས་ཅན་ཡིན་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བས་ནི་ཆོས་མཐུན་པའི་དཔེ་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་དཔེ་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འགྲོ་བ་པོ་དང་འགྲོ་བ་གཞན་པ་ཉིད་མ་
ཡིན་པའི་དཔེའོ། །དེའི་དབང་གིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབང་གིས་དཔེ་བསྟན་དགོས་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དཔེ་དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེ་ན། དེའི་ཕྱིར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཆོས་ཅན་ཡིན་པར་སྟོན་ཏོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨྲས་ཏེ། བསྒྲུབ་
པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཡིན་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེ་ན། སྐབས་འདིར་ནི་གཞན་པ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་པར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་རྒོལ་བ་དང་ཕྱིར་རྒོལ་བ་གཉི་ག་ལ་གྲགས་པ་ཡིན་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་
ཞེས་བྱའོ། །སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འགྲོ་བ་པོ་དང་འགྲོ་བ་གཞན་པ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེ་ན། སྐབས་འདིར་ནི་བརྗོད་པ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་འཇུག་པའི་ལྟོས་པ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་པར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་རྒོལ་བ་དང་ཕྱིར་རྒོལ་
བ་གཉིས་ཀ་ལ་གྲགས་པ་ཡིན་པས་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཆོས་ཅན་དཔེར་བསྟན་དུ་རུང་བ་དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེ་ན། འགྲོ་བའི་རང་གི་བདག་ཉིད་དམ་འགྲོ་བ་པོའི་རང་གི་བདག་ཉིད་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་ཡང་
བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་གཉི་ག་ལ་གྲགས་པ་གཞན་པ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་། སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གཉི་ག་ལ་གྲགས་པ་བརྗོད་པ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་འཇུག་པའི་ལྟོས་པ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡོད་པས་དེའི་ཕྱིར། དཔེ་ནི་དེའི་དབང་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཆོས་གྲགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་
ཆོས་ཅན་ཡིན་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་སོ། །འདིར་སྦྱོར་བའི་ཚིག་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འགྲོ་བ་པོ་དང་འགྲོ་བ་གཞན་པ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟན་པ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་སྐབས་འདིར་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་གཏན་ཚིགས་དང་དཔེ་དང་ལྡན་པས་སྦྱོར་བའི་ཚིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་བ་ནི་འོག་ནས་ཆོས་ཅན་དང་། བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ཆོས་

<meta>The text is part of a dialectical analysis concerning the relationship between the goer and the act of going, following Buddhist logic traditions.</meta>

The specific quality to be proven is called "not being a separate entity" <note>Tibetan: gzhan pa nyid ma yin pa</note>. The example is shown to be a subject that possesses both the quality to be proven and the proving quality, based on their established renown. This demonstrates the example of similarity. Regarding this, the "example" refers to the case where the goer and the act of going are not separate entities. 

The phrase "by the power of that" means the example must be shown through the power of the quality to be proven <note>the predicate of the thesis</note> and the proving quality <note>the reason or evidence</note>. What then is this example? It is stated that it "is shown to be a subject possessing the quality to be proven and the proving quality which are well-known." 

The "well-known quality to be proven" means the predicate itself is the quality. In this specific context, it should be applied as "not being a separate entity." Because this is well-known to both the proponent and the opponent, it is called the "well-known quality to be proven." 

The "well-known proving quality" <note>the logical reason</note> refers to the evidence that proves the goer and the act of going are not separate. In this context, it should be applied as "having a dependence on the occurrence of a specific expression." Because this is well-known to both the proponent and the opponent, it is called the "well-known proving quality." 

What is this subject that is suitable to be shown as an example, possessing both the well-known quality to be proven and the proving quality? It is the nature of the act of going itself, or the nature of the goer. In that case, there exists the quality to be proven well-known to both parties, "not being a separate entity," and the proving quality well-known to both parties, "having a dependence on the occurrence of a specific expression." Therefore, it is said that "the example is shown to be a subject possessing the quality to be proven and the proving quality which are well-known." 

The phrase "here, the syllogistic formulation" <note>Tibetan: sbyor ba'i tshig</note> refers to this context of proving that the goer and the act of going are not separate entities. The formulation that consists of an inference, a reason, and an example will be explained below, concerning the subject and the quality to be proven...

<summary>This page explains the logical structure of a syllogism used to prove that a traveler and the act of traveling are not separate entities. It defines the roles of the example, the predicate, and the logical reason within the context of Buddhist formal logic.</summary>
<keywords>syllogism, logic, goer, going, predicate, reason, example, non-difference</keywords>

གནས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་དེ་འགྲེལ་པས་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ། མཐོང་བའི་ལམ་ཐོབ་པས་མོས་པས་སྤྱོད་པའི་ས་དོར་བས་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་ས་ལས་འདས་པའོ། །ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་
སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ལས་འདས་པ་ནི་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ནམ་མཁའི་དཀྱིལ་དང་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་མཐོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ཏོ། །ཀུན་དུ་སྦྱོར་བ་གསུམ་སྤངས་པ་བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། དེའི་ཚེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་
སོགས་པ་ལ་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཐོང་བས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལས་ཐ་དད་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་རྟག་པ་ཉིད་ལ་སོགས་པ་མུ་སྟེགས་པས་སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པའི་བདག་མེད་པ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་པས་འཇིག་ཚོགས་ལ་ལྟ་བ་ལྡོག་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལ་འཇིག་ཚོགས་ལ་ལྟ་བ་ནི་
རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཏེ། མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱེད་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་དང་། ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པའོ། །དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །འདིར་གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱེད་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ལྡོག་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཐོང་བ་དང་དེའི་
ཕྱིར་ཐེ་ཚོམ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཐེ་ཚོམ་མེད་པས་ལམ་གཞན་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཅན་ལ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་བརྟུལ་ཞུགས་མཆོག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །སླར་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འབའ་ཞིག་ལྡོག་པ་ཡང་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡང་ཡོད་དེ། དཔེར་ན་རིམས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ཀུན་དུ་སྦྱོར་བ་
གསུམ་པོ་འདི་འགགས་ན་ཡང་སྐྱེ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ལྡོག་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མ་མཐོང་བ་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མ་མཐོང་བ་ནི་བདག་མེད་པ་ཉིད་མ་མཐོང་ནས་སོ། །གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མཐོང་ནའོ། །
ད་ནི་དགའ་བ་མཆོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་འཆང་ཞིང་། །ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ངེས་པ་ལ་ཞུས་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྨོས་ཏེ། ངེས་པ་ནི་མཐོང་བའི་ལམ་མོ། །དེའི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་གྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐོབ་པ་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཐོང་བའི་ལམ་གྱི་རྒྱུ་ཅན་གྱི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་གཅིག་ལ་

<meta>continues from previous page: this text continues a commentary on the stages of the Bodhisattva path, specifically focusing on the first level known as The Joyous.</meta>

It is stated, "he abides," and so forth. In order for the commentary to explain that verse, it says, "with the ordinary beings," and so forth. By attaining the path of seeing, one abandons the stage of practicing through aspiration and thus transcends the stage of an <term>ordinary being</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: prithagjana; a person who has not yet realized the truth of selflessness</gloss>. The transcendence of the stages of the <term>Listeners</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: Shravakas</gloss> and <term>Solitary Realizers</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: Pratyekabuddhas</gloss> has already been explained previously. The phrase "of the Tathagatas" <gloss>Thus Gone Ones; Buddhas</gloss> and so forth, is used because he sees all phenomena as equal to the center of space.

To explain the abandonment of the three fetters, the text says, "at that time," and so forth. The phrase "by perceiving the selflessness of the person directly" means that by directly seeing the absence of a self—which is imagined by the <term>outsiders</term> <gloss>non-Buddhist extremists</gloss> to be permanent and distinct from the aggregates—the view of the transitory collection is reversed. 

Regarding that, there are two types of views of the transitory collection: those arising from conceptual labeling and those that are co-emergent <gloss>innate</gloss>. These have also been explained before. Here, by the power of the specific occasion, it is the view arising from conceptual labeling that is reversed. Because he sees the selflessness of the person directly, he is therefore without doubt. Because he is without doubt, he also lacks the grasping at ethics and ascetic observances characterized by relying on other paths. 

The phrase "because they do not arise again" means that while some reversals of conditions can recur—for instance, like a fever—when these three fetters have ceased, they will not arise again. To show this through the method of reversal, the text says, "not seeing reality," and so forth. "Not seeing reality" refers to not seeing selflessness itself. The phrase "it is not otherwise" means when reality is seen.

Now, to explain the meaning of the phrase "he possesses supreme joy," the text says, "by entering into the certainty," and so forth. "Certainty" refers to the path of seeing. The phrase "attaining the qualities caused by that" refers to the attainment of one hundred concentrations caused by the path of seeing.

<summary>This page explains the transition from an ordinary being to a Bodhisattva on the path of seeing, specifically detailing the abandonment of the three fetters and the realization of selflessness. It defines the "certainty" of the path of seeing as the cause for supreme joy and advanced meditative qualities.</summary>
<keywords>path of seeing, selflessness, three fetters, ordinary being, transitory collection, certainty, joy, Bodhisattva levels</keywords>

Physical actions are like an optical illusion <note>original: "mig yor", also translated as a mirage or shimmering vision</note>. Although all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of inherent activity, physical actions appear just like an optical illusion. The phrase "like an echo" refers to the nature of vocal actions. Just as an echo lacks a core essence, speech enters the path of sound in the same way.

The phrase "like the moon in water" refers to the phenomena of the <term>Desire Realm</term> <gloss>Kamadhatu</gloss>. Just as the moon is reflected in water, the karmic ripening of past actions appears; it arises in accordance with the specific nature of the karma, just like the reflection of the moon in water.

The phrase "like an image" refers to the phenomena of the <term>Form Realm</term> <gloss>Rupadhatu</gloss> and the <term>Formless Realm</term> <gloss>Arupyadhatu</gloss>. These are equal to an image because their forms appear within the meditative concentration of those practicing in the Form and Formless realms. For that reason, one should say that they "enter into meditative equipoise" because they bring about this state of equality.

The phrase "equality like a magical emanation" refers to the nature of the completely pure Buddha-fields. These are equal to emanations because they are emanated through the complete purity of one's own mind.

Furthermore, the internal elements are like an illusion; even though there are no truly existent sentient beings, they appear with the nature of sentient beings. The external elements are like a dream; even though they are false <note>the text notes a variant spelling: brdzun/rdzun</note> in nature like a dream, the objects still appear.

The physical body of the Buddha, adorned with the marks of a Great Being and other qualities, is like an optical illusion because it appears from the completely pure <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss>. Everything contained within the revealed Doctrine <note>the Dharma</note> is like an echo, because like an echo, it is heard through the power of the Blessed One.

All results brought about by previous karma are like the moon in water, because they arise exactly according to the nature of the karma. Those things included in the completely pure Buddha-fields are like an image, because they appear in the mirror of the mind which is free from the stains of obscurations, just like a reflected image. All conditioned things…

<summary>This page explains the classic Buddhist analogies for emptiness—such as mirages, echoes, and reflections—applying them specifically to the three realms of existence and the attributes of a Buddha. It emphasizes that while phenomena appear to the mind based on karma and meditative states, they lack inherent substance.</summary>
<keywords>emptiness, twelve similes, Desire Realm, Form Realm, Buddha-fields, Dharmakaya, karma, meditative equipoise</keywords>

<meta>The text is a commentary on Madhyamaka philosophy, specifically refuting the identity of the self with the five aggregates, likely from Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra-bhāṣya or a related sub-commentary.</meta>

Therefore, as it is said, "The self is its own protector" <note>original: "bdag nyid bdag gi mgon yin gyi"</note>, because the word "self" <gloss>atman</gloss> is used there to refer to the mind alone. Thus, it is said that the object of focus for the view of the transitory collection <note>the view that believes in a permanent self within the changing aggregates of body and mind; Sanskrit: satkāyadṛṣṭi</note> is the mind alone. To provide an answer to that, it is said:

If the aggregates were the self <note>original: "gal te phung po bdag na"</note>, this means if the aggregates were exactly the self. Because they are many <note>original: "de mang bas"</note>, it means because the aggregates are numerous. Those selves would also become many <note>original: "bdag de dag kྱang mang por 'gyur"</note>. Because the aggregates and the self would be inseparable, the self would also become many, but you do not accept it that way either. The self would become a substance <note>original: "bdag ni rdzas su 'gyur zhing"</note>, which means that because the self is inseparable from the aggregates, and because the aggregates exist as substances <gloss>dravya</gloss>, it follows that the self would also exist as a substance. The view in that case <note>original: "der lta ba"</note> means regarding it as inseparable from the aggregates. Furthermore, you do not accept that the self exists as a substance. By engaging with a substance, it would not be a misconception <note>original: "rdzas la 'jug pas phyin ci log mi 'gyur"</note>. This means that the view of the transitory collection would focus on a self characterized by the five aggregates, and by focusing on a substance, it would not be a mistaken view.

To show this through the commentary, it is said: "The self would also become many," because it is inseparable from the aggregates. According to that view as well <note>original: "de'i ltar na yang"</note>, it refers to the view of those who assert that consciousness is a substance <note>referring to the Cittamatra or Mind-Only school</note>. By the divisions of consciousness such as the eye and so on <note>original: "mig la sogs pa'i rnam par shes pa'i dbye bas sam"</note>, it means that because the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousnesses are many, the self which is inseparable from them would also logically follow to be many. Because many consciousnesses arise and cease in every moment <note>original: "skad cig re re la rnam par shes pa skye ba dang 'gag pa mang ba'i phyir"</note>, it means that even each individual consciousness, such as the eye-consciousness, arises and ceases in every moment. Therefore, the self inseparable from them would also be many. Furthermore, the fault should be stated as appropriate: "If the aggregates were the self, then because they are many, those selves would also become many." This text regarding the aggregates <unclear>ends abruptly at the page break</unclear>.

<summary>This page presents a logical refutation of the idea that the self is identical to the five aggregates or the mind, arguing that if they were the same, the self would be multiple and momentary rather than single and permanent.</summary>

ཞིང་ཁམས་ཐམས་ཅད་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་པའི་རྣམ་འཕྲུལ་དང་། སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་འཇིག་པ་དང་། ཆགས་པ་དག་སྟོན་ཅིང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་འཕེལ་བར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་བས་སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་འགྲིབ་པར་མི་འགྱུར་

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>and so forth is spoken. By the word "and so forth," it is meant that he simultaneously manifests bodies according to the various inclinations of those to be trained. With a single cross-legged posture, he pervades all world-realms. Within each minute atom of his own body and each external minute atom, he displays all the world-realms, the miraculous displays of the conduct of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the destruction and formation of the realms of sentient beings. Because those minute atoms do not increase in size, the Buddhas and others likewise do not decrease in size, nor do they become mixed together. Even here, they remain intermingled just as in the vast Buddha-fields. Such are the activities of the body.

Furthermore, one should include the activities of speech, such as teaching the Dharma with a single word according to the various inclinations of those to be trained, pervading all world-realms with a single word, and the appearance of all melodies within a single melody. One should also include the activities of the mind, such as accomplishing immeasurable meditative absorptions through a single <term>samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss>.

Thus, having shown the qualities of the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the tenth ground <note>the tenth bhumi or stage of a Bodhisattva's path</note>, the text now states "following that" and so forth, in order to show the qualities of the state of Buddhahood. "Following that" means after the description of the qualities of the Bodhisattvas. The phrase "wishing to describe just a few qualities" means wanting to show some of the qualities, for it is impossible to describe the qualities without exception. For that very reason, it will be explained starting with the phrase "the Buddha, the Blessed One himself." "By way of accomplishing praise" means by way of describing the qualities as they truly are. 

In that regard, in order to show praise by way of possessing the perfection of abandonment <note>the total removal of all obscurations and negative tendencies</note> and the perfection of realization, the text says "just as" and so forth. Just as the moon on the fifteenth day <note>the full moon</note> shines in a stainless sky...

<summary>This page describes the miraculous physical, verbal, and mental activities of a tenth-level Bodhisattva before transitioning to discuss the even greater, indescribable qualities of a fully enlightened Buddha.</summary>

རྩོད་པ་བཟློག་པའི་ཚིག་ལེའུར་བྱས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ། འཇམ་དཔལ་གཞོན་ནུར་གྱུར་པ་ལ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དངོས་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི། །རང་བཞིན་ཀུན་ལ་ཡོད་མིན་ན། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་ཚིག་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་མེད། །རང་བཞིན་བཟློག་པར་མི་ནུས་སོ། །འོན་ཏེ་ཚིག་དེ་རང་བཞིན་བཅས། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་
དམ་བཅའ་སྔ་མ་ཉམས། །མི་འདྲ་ཉིད་དེ་དེ་ཡིན་ན། །ཁྱད་པར་གཏན་ཚིགས་བརྗོད་པར་གྱིས། །དེ་སྒྲ་མ་འབྱིན་ལྟ་བུའོ་ཞེས། །ཁྱོད་བློ་སེམས་ན་དེ་མི་འཐད། །འདི་ལ་སྒྲ་ནི་ཡོད་པ་ཡིས། །འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་བཟློག་ཡིན། །འགོག་པའི་འགོག་པའང་དེ་ལྟ་ཞེས། །འདོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་
བཟང་མིན་ཏེ། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་དམ་བཅའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ལས། །དེ་ལྟར་སྐྱོན་ཡོད་ངེད་ལ་མེད། །རེ་ཞིག་གལ་ཏེ་མངོན་སུམ་གྱིས#། །དངོས་རྣམས་དམིགས་ནས་ཟློག་#བྱེད་པ། །གང་གིས་དངོས་རྣམས་དམིགས་འགྱུར་བ། །མངོན་སུམ་དེ་ནི་མེད་པ་ཡིན། །རྗེས་དཔག་ལུང་དང་དཔེར་#འཇལ་དང་། །རྗེས་དཔག་

This translation was written by comparing the versions of the translators <term>Zhönnu Chok</term>, <term>Nyendarma Drak</term>, and <term>Khu</term>, selecting the best meanings and expressions.

### The Verses of the Refutation of Objections

In the language of India: <term>Vigrahavyāvartanī-kārikā-nāma</term>
In the language of Tibet: <term>rTsod pa bzlog pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa zhes bya ba</term>

Homage to Manjushri, the Youthful.

If the intrinsic nature of all things
Does not exist in anything at all,
Then your own words lack intrinsic nature,
And cannot refute intrinsic nature.

However, if those words possess intrinsic nature,
Your previous proposition is ruined.
Since there is such a lack of uniformity,
You must provide a specific logical reason.

If you think in your mind, "It is like
Telling someone not to make a sound," that is incorrect.
In that case, the sound that is actually present
Refutes the sound that will arise.

If you claim the refutation of my refutation is the same,
That is also not a good argument.
Such a fault exists within the definition of your proposition,
But it does not exist in mine.

Furthermore, if you refute things
By perceiving them through direct perception,
Then that direct perception by which 
Things are perceived does not exist.

The same response given to direct perception
Applies to inference, scripture, and analogy,
As well as to the objects to be proven 
By inference, scripture, or analogy.

Worldly people skilled in the states of phenomena
Think that virtuous phenomena
Possess a virtuous intrinsic nature;
And so they think for the remaining types.

Those phenomena that lead to liberation,
Which are spoken of as states of phenomena,
Would have an intrinsic nature of leading to liberation,
Rather than lacking such a nature.

If phenomena have no intrinsic nature,
Even the phrase "lack of intrinsic nature"
And the name itself would not exist,
Because there is no name without a basis.

If you say an intrinsic nature exists,
But it does not exist within phenomena,
Then you ought to show what that intrinsic nature is
Aside from the phenomena themselves.

Because the negation "There is no pot in the house"

Likewise, your negation would only be possible

<meta>The text continues the philosophical analysis of the relationship between an agent (creator) and the action (work), specifically examining the logical impossibilities of their transition between states of existence and non-existence.</meta>

Furthermore, a transition does not occur. An agent who already exists does not create something that is non-existent. An agent who is non-existent does not create something that is existent. Why is this? Because in this case, the same logical fallacies mentioned previously would follow.

If one investigates the nature of such an agent and such an action, the faults previously explained would apply here as well. Specifically, if the agent already exists, the action becomes redundant. If the action exists, the agent becomes unnecessary. If the action is non-existent, it lacks an agent. If the agent and the action are both non-existent, they would lack a cause. Therefore, an agent who exists does not create what is non-existent, and an agent who is non-existent does not create what is existent.

Regarding the agent and the action:
One who exists does not create what is non-existent,
Nor what is both existent and non-existent.

An agent who exists does not create an action that is non-existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent. Why is this? It is because the logical reasons have been explained above. If the agent exists, the action is redundant; if the action is non-existent, it lacks a cause; and since being existent and non-existent are mutually exclusive, how could they be one and the same? This is what is demonstrated.

Regarding the agent and the action:
One who is non-existent does not create what is existent,
Nor what is both existent and non-existent.

An agent who is non-existent does not create an action that is existent, nor one that is both existent and non-existent. Why is this? It is because the logical reasons have been explained above. From a non-existent agent, the result would be causeless. For a non-existent action, there is no activity. Furthermore, since being existent and non-existent are mutually exclusive, how could they be one and the same? This is what is demonstrated.

An agent who is both existent and non-existent
Does not create an action that is existent or non-existent.

An agent who is both existent and non-existent does not create an action that is existent, nor one that is non-existent. Why is this? In this case too, the logical reasons should be understood as explained above. Because an agent who is both existent and non-existent involves mutual contradictions, how could such a thing be one? If the action were existent, activity would be redundant; if the action were non-existent, it would be without a cause. This is what is demonstrated.

<summary>This page presents a dialectical critique of the causal relationship between an agent and their action, arguing that production is impossible regardless of whether the participants are existent, non-existent, or both. It relies on the principle that mutually exclusive states cannot coexist and that existent things do not require further creation.</summary>
<keywords>Middle Way, Madhyamaka, agent and action, existence and non-existence, causality, logical fallacy, Derge Tengyur, Nagarjuna</keywords>

When one utters only these words, it is like this example: if one tells a person born blind that a certain direction is safe, they cannot see because they lack eyes. They will become confused and stumble. Similarly, even if one says that this world does not exist, one will be stained by faults because they cannot see, for they lack the eye of wisdom.

Furthermore, consider an example of a legal dispute where two witnesses are produced to establish the truth of a matter. One witness has actually seen the matter directly. The second witness has not seen the matter directly but is motivated by personal gain or friendship. When both are made to testify about the matter, even if the first person speaks the truth as it is, if they had not seen it directly, their testimony could still become a <term>falsehood</term> <gloss>original: rdzun</gloss>. It would be associated with unrighteousness and a bad reputation. The other witness, in speaking of the matter, is a speaker of truth because they saw it directly. They are associated with righteousness and a good reputation.

In the same way, all things are empty. Because they are empty, they are unproduced and unceasing. Even so, only the person who has direct perception of this is endowed with goodness and praise. The other person is stained by the faults of wrong views because emptiness has not become a direct perception for them. They will be criticized by the wise. Therefore, there is a very great difference between these two.

As the master <term>Rahulabhadra</term> <gloss>original: sgra gcan zin bzang po</gloss> said in his <term>Praise to the Perfection of Wisdom</term> <gloss>original: shes rab kྱི་ phar rol tu phyin pa la bstod pa</gloss>:

Seeing you, one is bound;
Not seeing you, one is also bound.
Seeing you, one is freed;
Not seeing you, one is also freed.

This is the object of an eye of intelligence that is stainless and knows reality as it is. It is not the object for one whose eye of intelligence is obscured by the great darkness of ignorance. Furthermore, your very pride in being wise...

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of direct realization of emptiness over mere intellectual or verbal understanding. It uses analogies of a blind man and legal witnesses to show that speaking the truth without direct experience can still lead to error and negative consequences.</summary>

If awareness is not realized, then there will be no thorough understanding of existence <term>samsara</term> and liberation <term>nirvana</term>. Without thorough understanding, the fruit of attaining the abandonment of these states will not arise. For this very reason, the text states:

->All those of excellent intelligence exert themselves in inner contemplation.<-

This means that whoever possesses excellent intelligence is called one of excellent intelligence. All such individuals of excellent intelligence exert themselves in the contemplation of the inner self, the mind. The term inner refers to inner awareness. Contemplation refers to the acts of hearing, thinking, and meditating. Exertion means striving for that purpose; it means that which is cultivated through familiarization. The meaning is that by doing so, they will achieve an unerring and thorough understanding of existence and liberation.

Now, following the scriptural tradition, the characteristics of the states of the sutras regarding cyclic existence and liberation are summarized by stating:

->Mind along with the stains of desire and so forth.<-

Desire refers to those who initially possess attachment. By stating and so forth, hatred, delusion, and the rest are included. Through the power of habitual tendencies, the mind that is permeated by the stains of desire and the rest is called cyclic existence <term>samsara</term>. When that very mind is made devoid of desire and the rest through the meditation on the path, it is summarized and taught—not in an extensive way—as liberation <term>nirvana</term>.

Who taught this? The text states:

->By the Victors who have abandoned the obscurations.<-

Those who have abandoned the obscurations of afflictive emotions and the obscurations to knowledge are the ones who have abandoned the obscurations. The meaning is that such beings have taught this.

Lest it be certain that desire and the rest exist in an ultimate sense, the text states the following to negate that:

->Desire, hatred, and delusion.<-

Embodied beings are those possessing a body. Whatever desire, hatred, and delusion exist, they should be understood as being of the nature of mere mental conceptualization. Therefore, they do not exist in an ultimate sense.

<summary>This page explains that liberation depends on inner awareness and the realization that cyclic existence is defined by a mind stained by desire, hatred, and delusion. It emphasizes that these afflictions are ultimately mere conceptual constructs rather than inherently real entities.</summary>

<keywords>awareness, samsara, nirvana, excellent intelligence, contemplation, desire, hatred, delusion, obscurations, mental conceptualization</keywords>

The measurement of the three celestial palaces, such as the first <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>state of meditative concentration</gloss>, is equal to the measurement of a small thousandfold universe. Some say that the celestial palace of the fourth meditative state is immeasurable. Gods born in the lower realms do not see the celestial palaces of the higher realms. However, gods born in higher realms certainly see the palaces of the lower realms. One may travel upward by means of <term>riddhi</term> <gloss>miraculous powers</gloss> or by relying on someone possessing such powers. Those born in higher realms may come down and see, but this does not apply to the higher realms themselves. It is also said that one cannot see that which is called a higher level.

The <term>Arupyadhatu</term> <gloss>Formless Realm</gloss> consists of four levels and four spheres of totality. These are the level of the sphere of infinite space, the level of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the level of the sphere of nothingness, and the level of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception. There are also the corresponding spheres of totality for infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither perception nor non-perception.

The limits of such world systems do not exist; there are as many world systems as there are reaches of space. These arrangements of world systems do not exist with gaps or intervals between the ten directions, above, or below. World systems are constantly in the process of disintegrating or forming. It is said that the Desire Realm exists even above the <term>Akanistha</term> <gloss>Highest Pure Land</gloss>, and the <term>Akanistha</term> also exists below the Desire Realm.

I shall now describe the measurements above and below the twenty-three abodes, starting from the realm of the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the limit of the <term>Akanistha</term>. Specifically, the fourth terrace is the fundamental abode of the Four Great Kings, located forty thousand <term>yojana</term> <gloss>leagues</gloss> from here. From there, the abode of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is as far above as the distance to Jambudvipa below. Again, below that is Jambudvipa...

<summary>This page describes the cosmological structure and dimensions of the Meditative and Formless Realms. It details the visibility between higher and lower divine abodes and the infinite nature of world systems in space.</summary>

པ་གཅིག་ཉིད་དེ་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། ཡིད་ཀྱི་འདུས་ཏེ་རེག་པའོ། །ཡང་རེག་པ་ལ་གསུམ་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། རིག་པའི་རེག་པ་དང་། མ་རིག་པའི་རེག་པ་དང་། རིག་པ་མ་ཡིན་མ་རིག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་རེག་པའོ། །ཡང་རེག་པ་ལ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་པའི་རེག་པ་དང་། ཉོན་
མོངས་པ་ཅན་གྱི་རེག་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་པ་ནི། རིག་པའི་རེག་པའོ། །ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཅན་ནི་མ་རིག་པའི་རེག་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་མ་རིག་པའི་རེག་པ་ལ་གཉིས་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། གནོད་སེམས་ཀྱི་རེག་པ་དང་། རྗེས་སུ་ཆགས་པའི་རེག་པའོ། །རིག་པ་མ་ཡིན་མ་རིག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་རེག་པ་ལ་
གཉིས་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། དགེ་བ་ཟག་བཅས་ཀྱི་རེག་པ་དང་། སྒྲིབ་མིན་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་གྱི་རེག་པའོ། །ཡང་རེག་པ་ལ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་བར་བྱ་བའི་རེག་པ་དང་། བདེ་བ་མྱོང་བར་བྱ་བའི་རེག་པ་དང་། སྡུག་བསྔལ་མ་ཡིན་བདེ་བ་མ་ཡིན་པ་མྱོང་བར་བྱ་བའི་རེག་པའོ། །རེག་པའི་
ཡན་ལག་གོ། །ཚོར་བ་ལ་དྲུག་ནི་འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ། མིག་གི་འདུས་ཏེ་རེག་པ་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཚོར་བ་དང་། རྣ་བ་དང་ཕྲད་པ་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཚོར་བ་དང་། སྣ་དང་ཕྲད་པ་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཚོར་བ་དང་། ལྕེའི་འདུས་ཏེ་རེག་པ་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཚོར་བ་དང་། ལུས་ཀྱི་འདུས་ཏེ་རེག་པ་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཚོར་བ་དང་།
